In southern Argentina, across the vast expanses of Patagonia, Los Glaciares National Park is a remarkable world of glaciers, mountain peaks, turquoise lakes and wildlife. Here, the rugged beauty of the Andes meets the pristine allure of icy landscapes, creating scenery that stays with travelers long after their journey.

The park's greatest treasure is its enormous glaciers, fed by the ice fields of the Southern Andes. Their snow-white slopes descend into deep valleys, while sculpted walls of ice are reflected in mountain lakes. The park's best-known natural wonder is Perito Moreno Glacier, celebrated for its immense size, vivid blue ice and constant movement. From viewing platforms, visitors can watch huge blocks break away from the glacier's face and crash into Lake Argentino with a thunderous roar.

The mountain country around El Chaltén reveals another side of Los Glaciares. The famous peaks of Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre rise above the valleys, drawing mountaineers and hikers from around the world. Trails lead through southern beech forests, alongside mountain rivers and lakes, to viewpoints with spectacular vistas of rocky summits and glaciers. On clear days, the peaks seem to emerge from the clouds, forming one of Patagonia's most recognizable landscapes.

The national park's wildlife is equally compelling. Guanacos, Andean condors and numerous other representatives of Patagonian fauna can be encountered in the surrounding area. The natural ecosystems retain their distinctive character, while the open spaces and silence offer a welcome escape from the bustle of city life.

Los Glaciares is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized for the exceptional natural value of its glacial landscapes. Visitors can set out on a mountain hike, get close to ancient masses of ice, take a boat trip on a lake or simply admire the grandeur of the Andes.

A journey to Los Glaciares is an encounter with one of South America's most impressive natural areas, where ice, water, mountains and wind come together in an unforgettable Patagonian landscape.

The plains of Los Llanos stretch for hundreds of kilometers, covering almost a third of Venezuela. They form an immense savanna, interrupted here and there by isolated grasslands and groves. The Río Apure roughly divides the region in two, separating the Llanos Altos ("upper" or elevated plains) from the Llanos Bajos (the "low" plains).

The llaneros, the people of this region, earn their living by raising livestock. Much like the cowboys of the American West, they are known for their exceptional horsemanship and skill as cattle herders.

During the rainy season (July–November), much of the Llanos is flooded, and only a few roads built on raised embankments remain relatively dry. In the dry season, the land dries out quickly and wildlife gathers around ponds and streams. The sheer abundance and diversity of wildlife are extraordinary: the region is home to anacondas, caimans, river dolphins, jaguars, pumas, capybaras, monkeys, anteaters, numerous hoofed animals and an enormous variety of birds.

Los Roques is an archipelago of 346 large and small islands. A national park was established across the archipelago in 1972, placing its 24-kilometer coral reef under state protection.

Many of the islands remain closed to tourists, but those that are accessible offer the pleasure of exploring remarkably unspoiled tropical nature. You can go diving or snorkeling to see colorful fish in their natural habitat. If you prefer to watch marine life in a more relaxed setting, you can take a trip in a glass-bottomed boat. Both experiences leave lasting memories and stories to share when you return home.

## Three volcanoes in western El Salvador

Los Volcanes National Park encompasses the Santa Ana, Izalco and [Cerro Verde](/el-salvador/place/cerro-verde/) volcanoes. Together they form a single natural region, yet their landscapes are strikingly different: forested slopes meet dark volcanic rock and exposed cones. Even a sightseeing trip therefore reveals several distinct panoramas.

## Panoramas, forests and hiking

Around Cerro Verde, walking trails and viewpoints offer opportunities to spend time among mountain vegetation and see the neighboring peaks without a long ascent.

Climbing Santa Ana or Izalco involves separate routes that require suitable physical fitness and arranged guidance. A general visit to the park does not in itself mean that an ascent of every summit is included.

## What to combine with your visit

Los Volcanes pairs well with [Lake Coatepeque](/el-salvador/place/lake-coatepeque/): volcanic panoramas and time by the water reveal different sides of the same region.

On the [Best of El Salvador](/el-salvador/tour/el-salvador-san-salvador-suchitoto-gulf-of-fonseca/) tour, the park is visited on the second day, after El Boquerón. The itinerary then continues along the [Route of Flowers](/el-salvador/place/ruta-de-las-flores/) through the coffee-growing region of western El Salvador.
